word_order: SOV — verbs consistently appear clause-finally, e.g. sentence 6 'ごんは家の裏口から、こっそり中へはいりました' (Gon ... quietly entered), object/locative phrases precede the verb 'はいりました'.
punctuation_present: always — every sentence ends in 。 and uses 、 for internal pauses; dialogue uses 「」
register: read-aloud narrative prose (classic Japanese children's literature / storybook style, past-tense narration with embedded dialogue)
clause_boundary_signals: ました/でした (past-tense sentence-final predicates)
と (quotative particle before 思う/言う, marks end of quoted clause)
から (causal, marks subordinate clause end)
ますと/たら/ば (conditional connectives, mark clause boundary before main clause)
non_boundary_traps: て-form verbs (e.g. 思って, 立ちあがって) — connect to a following clause, not a stopping point
、 comma after te-form or nominalized phrase — very frequent but usually NOT a safe split point
の (nominalizer/possessive) — looks sentence-final-ish but often continues into a copula or another clause
ながら (while) — subordinate marker, clause continues after it
と before 思う/言う — quotative particle, do not split before the verb of saying/thinking
ようとしましたが — volitional + but, mid-clause connector, not a full stop
target_language_risks: Japanese and Korean are both SOV/head-final, but topic markers (は) and subject/object particles (が/を) do not map 1:1 onto Korean particles, so splitting before the verb can strand a particle-marked NP without its predicate
Honorific/politeness level of the sentence-final verb (ました/でした) is only resolved at the clause end; splitting mid-clause can produce Korean output with mismatched register
Quoted speech in 「」 needs the following 思う/言う verb to know if it's direct speech or reported thought; premature segmentation loses this control
Long te-form chains (V-te, V-te, V-ta) form one semantic event chain in Japanese; Korean connective endings (-고, -서) require knowing the final verb's tense/aspect before translating earlier clauses
Omitted subjects (common in Japanese) must be inferred from prior context; segmenting too early forces premature guessing of the subject in Korean
notes_for_prompt_writer: Treat 。and closing 」as hard, safe segment boundaries; treat 、 as a soft signal that usually should NOT trigger a split because most clauses continue via te-form or nominalized connectors. Wait for the sentence-final predicate (ました/でした/です/だ) before closing a segment, since honorific level and tense are only fixed there. Be especially careful with quotative と before 思う/言う and with causal/conditional connectors (から, ので, たら, ば) — these mark real clause boundaries and are good candidates for earlier (but still safe) splitting points in a low-latency pipeline.
